events.title: The Praetorians auction the empire to Didius Julianus
events.summary: After murdering Pertinax on 28 March 193, the Praetorian Guard sold the throne to the senator Marcus Didius Julianus, who outbid Pertinax's father-in-law Flavius Sulpicianus with a promise of 25,000 sesterces per guardsman.
events.detail: Dio, an eyewitness senator, describes the bidding conducted from the walls of the Castra Praetoria, Sulpicianus inside the camp and Julianus shouting offers from outside. Julianus never won the urban plebs, who pelted him in the Circus and called on Pescennius Niger, and within two weeks three provincial armies had proclaimed their own commanders. The episode became the classic illustration of the Guard's power and directly prompted Severus to abolish the old Italian Praetorian cohorts.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.debate: Herodian and Dio dramatise the 'auction'; the HA life is late and partly derivative, but the core sequence is accepted.

events.title: Septimius Severus proclaimed emperor at Carnuntum
events.summary: Lucius Septimius Severus, legate of Pannonia Superior, was hailed Augustus by the Danube legions at Carnuntum, posing as the avenger of Pertinax and adding Pertinax to his name.
events.detail: Severus, an African senator from Lepcis Magna, could count on all sixteen legions of the Rhine and Danube. He marched on Rome so fast that Julianus' attempts to fortify the city, train elephants and send assassins collapsed. To secure his rear he offered the title of Caesar to Clodius Albinus in Britain, isolating Pescennius Niger in the East.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.title: Pescennius Niger proclaimed emperor at Antioch
events.summary: Gaius Pescennius Niger, governor of Syria, was acclaimed by the eastern legions and enjoyed the support of the Roman populace, but delayed in Antioch while Severus took Rome.
events.detail: Niger controlled nine legions and Egypt's grain, and won the backing of Antioch and, crucially, Byzantium, which controlled the Bosporus crossing. Parthian and client rulers (Hatra, Osroene, Adiabene) offered or promised help, giving Severus his pretext for the eastern wars of 195 and 197-198.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.debate: The HA life of Niger is among the most fictional in the collection (forged letters and documents).

events.title: Severus enters Rome and disbands the Praetorian Guard
events.summary: After the Senate condemned Julianus, who was killed in the palace on 1 June 193, Severus summoned the Praetorians unarmed, cashiered them and replaced them with a doubled guard drawn from his Danubian legionaries.
events.detail: The new Guard of ten milliary cohorts, with the Urban Cohorts and Vigiles also enlarged, made Rome a garrison city of perhaps 30,000 men once II Parthica was stationed at Albanum. Italians lost their near-monopoly on Guard service, a change Dio deplores as filling the capital with savage-looking soldiers. Severus deified Pertinax and staged a lavish funeral to legitimise himself.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.title: Clodius Albinus accepts the title of Caesar
events.summary: Decimus Clodius Albinus, governor of Britain with three legions, accepted Severus' offer of the rank of Caesar and coinage in his name, neutralising him while Severus dealt with Niger.
events.detail: Albinus, an aristocrat from Hadrumetum, struck coins as Caesar at Rome and held the consulship of 194 with Severus. The arrangement implied succession, a promise Severus cancelled in 195 when he made his elder son Caesar.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.title: Battle of Cyzicus
events.summary: Severan forces defeated and killed Niger's general Asellius Aemilianus near Cyzicus, opening Asia Minor to Severus.
events.detail: Niger had crossed into Europe and occupied Byzantium and Perinthus, but Severus' troops, crossing the Propontis elsewhere, caught Aemilianus, proconsul of Asia, near Cyzicus. Aemilianus was killed (Dio says while fleeing; Herodian hints he was already disloyal to Niger).

battle.significance: First major defeat for Niger; he withdrew behind the Taurus and the Cilician Gates.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.debate: Exact date (late 193 or early 194) uncertain; commander on the Severan side probably Ti. Claudius Candidus.

events.title: Siege of Byzantium
events.summary: Byzantium, having sided with Niger, held out against Severan forces for some two and a half years, surviving even after Niger's death until famine forced surrender in late 195.
events.detail: Dio gives a vivid account of the city's walls of squared stone bound with bronze plates, the engines of the engineer Priscus of Nicaea, and the citizens reduced to eating hides and finally each other. Severus executed the magistrates and soldiers, razed the walls, and subordinated the city to Perinthus as a village; it was soon rebuilt, reportedly at Caracalla's request.

sides.strength: citizens and Nigerian remnants; c. 500 small boats

battle.significance: Destroyed the walls guarding the Bosporus, which Dio later blamed for opening the straits to raiders.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.debate: Marius Maximus, later biographer of emperors and a lost source of the HA, commanded Moesian forces in the siege according to his career inscription.

events.title: Battle of Nicaea
events.summary: Niger in person was defeated by the Severan general Tiberius Claudius Candidus in the defiles between Cius and Nicaea, and retreated through the Cilician Gates.
events.detail: Dio describes a battle fought partly on the plain and partly in the narrows and on the lake of Ascania, with Niger's appearance briefly rallying his men. Candidus' victory exposed Bithynia and led cities such as Nicaea and Nicomedia to declare for opposite sides, a vivid sign of civic rivalry exploited in civil wars.

battle.significance: Drove Niger out of Asia Minor.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.title: Battle of Issus
events.summary: On the plain of Issus, where Alexander had beaten Darius, Severus' general Publius Cornelius Anullinus decisively defeated Pescennius Niger, whose army broke after a storm blew in its face.
events.detail: Niger's army held a strong position in the pass, but a cavalry force under Valerianus outflanked it through the woods while a thunderstorm, beating into the faces of Niger's men and at the backs of the Severans, was read as divine favour. Dio claims 20,000 of Niger's men died. Niger fled toward the Euphrates hoping to reach Parthia but was caught and beheaded near Antioch; his head was displayed before Byzantium to break its resistance.

battle.significance: Ended Niger's bid; the East passed to Severus, who punished Antioch and rewarded Laodicea.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.debate: Date usually spring 194; Dio's casualty figure is a round literary number. Both authors stress the Alexandrian echo.

events.title: Syria divided; Antioch humiliated
events.summary: After Niger's defeat Severus split Syria into Syria Coele and Syria Phoenice, stripped Antioch of its city status in favour of Laodicea, and punished other Nigerian cities.
events.detail: The division continued the Hadrianic and Antonine practice of reducing the number of legions under any single governor; Britain was likewise split into Superior and Inferior, probably early in the third century. Antioch was made a village of Laodicea and its Olympic games transferred, while Laodicea, Tyre and other loyal cities received colonial or metropolitan titles. Antioch's status was restored under Caracalla.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.debate: Date of the British division (197, c. 213 or later) disputed; Herodian 3.8.2 places it under Severus.

events.title: Severus' first eastern campaign: Osroene and Adiabene
events.summary: In 195 Severus crossed the Euphrates against Osroene, Adiabene and Arab allies who had supported Niger and besieged Nisibis, taking the titles Arabicus and Adiabenicus.
events.detail: Using the pretext of the clients' support for Niger, Severus based himself at Nisibis and sent columns across northern Mesopotamia. Much of Osroene was annexed, leaving the Abgarid king at Edessa with a rump. The campaign laid the groundwork for the province of Mesopotamia and was cut short by news of Albinus' defection. Severus refused the title Parthicus to avoid provoking Vologaeses.

events.title: Severus declares himself son of Marcus Aurelius
events.summary: Severus retroactively adopted himself into the Antonine house as 'divi Marci filius', renamed his son Bassianus Marcus Aurelius Antoninus (Caracalla) and made him Caesar, an open break with Albinus.
events.detail: The fiction, ridiculed by a senator who congratulated Severus on finding a father, gave the new dynasty Antonine legitimacy and allowed the rehabilitation of Commodus, deified as Severus' 'brother' in 197. Inscriptions trace Severus' lineage back to Nerva. The making of Caracalla Caesar, probably at Viminacium in 195 or 196, converted the agreement with Albinus into war.

events.title: Clodius Albinus proclaimed Augustus
events.summary: Cut out of the succession, Albinus was hailed Augustus by the British legions and crossed to Gaul, setting up his base at Lugdunum, where he minted coins; the Senate declared him a public enemy in December 196.
events.detail: Albinus had senatorial sympathy at Rome, where crowds at the Circus chanted against a new civil war. In Gaul he defeated the governor of Germania Inferior, Virius Lupus, but failed to win over the Rhine legions, which remained loyal to Severus.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.title: Battle of Lugdunum
events.summary: Severus defeated Clodius Albinus in a vast battle north of Lyon; Dio puts some 150,000 men on each side. Albinus committed suicide or was killed and his corpse was mutilated; Lugdunum was sacked.
events.detail: Albinus' left wing was routed, but his right lured Severus' men into concealed trenches and pits; Severus himself was unhorsed and threw off his purple cloak, and only the arrival of the cavalry under Julius Laetus decided the day (Dio insinuates Laetus had waited to see who was winning, and Severus later had him executed). Albinus' head was sent to Rome. Severus confiscated vast estates of Albinus' partisans in Gaul, Spain and Britain, creating the res privata as a major branch of imperial finance. Preliminary fighting took place near Tinurtium (Tournus), named in the HA.

sides.strength: c. 150,000 (Dio); British legions and Gallic recruits

battle.significance: The largest battle between Roman armies recorded; ended the civil wars of 193-197 and left Severus sole ruler.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.debate: Dio's 300,000 total is impossible for the forces available; modern estimates are far lower. The exact field is unknown.

events.title: Severus' purge of the Senate
events.summary: Returning to Rome in June 197, Severus praised the cruelty of Marius, Sulla and Augustus before the Senate and executed 29 senators accused of supporting Albinus, while sparing 35 others.
events.detail: Severus deified Commodus as his adoptive brother, a deliberate insult to senators who had hated him. The confiscations, together with those of Niger's partisans, filled the treasury and enabled the first pay rise for soldiers since Domitian.
events.debate: The HA lists 41 names, many probably invented.

events.title: Severan army reforms: pay, marriage and new legions
events.summary: Severus raised military pay (legionary stipendium probably from 300 to 450 or 500 denarii), allowed serving soldiers to marry legally, and raised three new legions, I, II and III Parthica, the latter two under equestrian prefects.
events.detail: Herodian attributes to Severus the dying advice to his sons to 'enrich the soldiers and scorn everyone else'. Legal marriage formalised long-standing unions in the canabae; centurions gained the right to wear the gold ring of equestrian rank. II Parthica's base at Albanum, 20 km from Rome, put a legion in Italy for the first time since Augustus, creating a central strategic reserve that anticipated later field armies. I and III Parthica garrisoned the new province of Mesopotamia at Singara and Rhesaina.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.debate: The size of the pay increase is reconstructed from papyri and Speidel's calculations; dates for the marriage concession range 197-200.

events.title: Parthian siege of Nisibis
events.summary: While Severus fought Albinus, Vologaeses V attacked the new Roman positions in Mesopotamia and besieged Nisibis, defended by Julius Laetus until Severus' arrival in summer 197 lifted the threat.

battle.significance: Gave Severus his casus belli for a full invasion of Parthia.

events.title: Severus sacks Ctesiphon
events.summary: Sailing down the Euphrates with a river fleet, Severus took Seleucia and Babylon, then stormed the Parthian capital Ctesiphon in late 197 or January 198, sacking it and, according to Dio, carrying off 100,000 captives.
events.detail: Vologaeses V fled. The sack, the third Roman capture of Ctesiphon in eighty years (Trajan 116, Avidius Cassius 165), was timed to the centenary of Trajan's accession and was celebrated with the title Parthicus Maximus on 28 January 198. Severus did not hold the city: supply failures forced a return up the Tigris. The repeated blows on Ctesiphon gravely weakened Arsacid prestige and are usually seen as a background cause of the Persian revolt of Ardashir a generation later.

sides.strength: perhaps 3 Parthian legions plus vexillations and a river fleet

battle.significance: Humiliated the Arsacids and made Mesopotamia a permanent Roman province.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.debate: Herodian makes the fleet's arrival at Ctesiphon accidental; Dio's captive total is implausibly round.

events.title: Caracalla raised to Augustus, Geta to Caesar
events.summary: On the centenary of Trajan's accession and the day of the victory proclamation over Parthia, Severus made the ten-year-old Caracalla co-Augustus and his younger son Geta Caesar.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.title: First Severan siege of Hatra
events.summary: Returning up the Tigris, Severus attacked Hatra, the walled Arab caravan city in the desert, but its engines and naphtha bombs burned his siege works and he withdrew.

battle.significance: Repeated Trajan's failure of 117 at the same city.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.debate: Herodian telescopes the two sieges into one; Dio distinguishes them.

events.title: Second Severan siege of Hatra
events.summary: Severus returned to Hatra in 199 with larger engines; when a breach was made, he called off the assault, hoping the city would surrender its treasure intact, but his exasperated European troops refused to renew the attack and the siege was abandoned after 20 days.
events.detail: Dio records that the Syrian troops ordered to attack were slaughtered and that Severus could not get his men to try again. The failure marked the limit of Severan expansion; Hatra later became a Roman ally with an attested Roman garrison (cohors IX Maurorum) in the 230s.

events.title: Creation of the province of Mesopotamia
events.summary: Severus organised northern Mesopotamia as a province under an equestrian prefect with legions I and III Parthica, centred on Nisibis, now a Roman colonia.
events.detail: Dio judged the province a source of constant wars and expense, a drain that drew Rome into every Persian quarrel. In fact Nisibis and Singara became the hinge of Roman-Persian conflict for 165 years until Jovian surrendered them in 363. Osroene was reduced to a rump client around Edessa and annexed in 213/214 and finally in 242.

events.title: Severus in Egypt; Alexandria receives a council
events.summary: Severus toured Egypt and Upper Egypt, visiting Memphis, Thebes and the 'singing' colossus of Memnon, and granted Alexandria and the metropoleis of the nomes town councils (boulai), a major change in Egyptian administration.
events.detail: The grant of councils, completed in 200/201, aligned Egypt with the civic organisation of the rest of the East and made councillors liable for tax collection. Severus is said to have repaired the Memnon colossus, after which it ceased to sing at dawn. He also issued responses to petitions (apokrimata) preserved on papyrus, a rare direct view of the emperor's justice.

events.title: Severus visits Africa; building at Lepcis and the Tripolitanian frontier
events.summary: Severus returned to his native Lepcis Magna, which received the ius Italicum, a new forum, basilica, colonnaded street and harbour, while the frontier of Tripolitania was pushed south with forts at Gholaia (Bu Njem), Gheriat and Cidamus (Ghadames).
events.debate: Whether Severus visited Africa in 202/203 is inferred from coins and the HA; Gholaia's foundation is dated 201 by inscription.

events.title: Martyrdom of Perpetua and Felicity at Carthage
events.summary: The young noblewoman Vibia Perpetua and her slave Felicitas, catechumens, were killed in the amphitheatre of Carthage at games for Geta's birthday; the Passio preserves Perpetua's own prison diary, the earliest surviving text by a Christian woman.
events.detail: The Passio Perpetuae records her dreams of a ladder to heaven and of fighting an Egyptian as a man, and her refusal of her pagan father's pleas. The text, possibly edited by a Montanist (Tertullian has been suggested), is a central document for women, martyrdom and North African Christianity. The HA claims Severus banned conversion to Judaism and Christianity, a statement most scholars doubt.
events.debate: Whether there was a general Severan persecution is rejected by most; prosecutions were local.

events.title: Arch of Septimius Severus dedicated in the Forum
events.summary: The Senate dedicated a triple arch at the foot of the Capitol celebrating the Parthian victories, with panels showing the sieges of Nisibis, Edessa, Seleucia and Ctesiphon; Geta's name was later erased from the inscription.

events.title: Secular Games of Septimius Severus
events.summary: Severus celebrated the seventh Ludi Saeculares in June 204, following the Augustan schedule of 110-year cycles; the acta, partly preserved on inscriptions, list Julia Domna leading 109 matrons in prayers.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.title: Fall of the praetorian prefect Plautianus
events.summary: Gaius Fulvius Plautianus, Severus' fellow Lepcitane and all-powerful praetorian prefect, whose daughter Plautilla had married Caracalla in 202, was accused of conspiracy and cut down in the palace in Caracalla's presence.
events.detail: Plautianus had accumulated statues, wealth and influence beyond any prefect since Sejanus; Dio says he castrated a hundred free Romans to attend his daughter. The plot charge was probably fabricated by Caracalla, who loathed his wife. Plautilla was exiled to Lipara and killed in 212. Papinian and Maecius Laetus replaced Plautianus, inaugurating the age of jurist-prefects.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.title: Bulla Felix's bandit band in Italy
events.summary: For two years the brigand Bulla Felix and 600 followers plundered Italy, freeing imperial slaves and robbing travellers under the noses of the emperors, until he was betrayed by a mistress and thrown to the beasts.
events.detail: Dio attributes to Bulla a Robin Hood maxim to the praetorian prefect Papinian, telling him to 'feed your slaves, so they won't turn bandit'. The episode, whatever its embellishment, reflects rural insecurity and the absorption of runaway and underpaid imperial slaves.

events.title: Severus' expedition to Britain and Caledonia
events.summary: Severus, his sons and the court moved to Britain in 208, made Eboracum the imperial capital and campaigned deep into Caledonia in 209 and 210 against the Caledonii and Maeatae, building a legionary base at Carpow on the Tay.
events.detail: Dio reports 50,000 Roman casualties from ambush and disease, a figure probably inflated. The Maeatae and Caledonians submitted in 209 and revolted in 210, when Severus ordered genocide ('let no one escape sheer destruction', quoting Homer). Coins of 210-211 proclaim VICTORIAE BRITTANNICAE. Hadrian's Wall was heavily restored in this period, and Severus' death in February 211 ended the project of conquest; Caracalla made peace and withdrew to the wall.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.debate: Whether Severus intended permanent conquest of all Scotland or a punitive war is debated; the Carpow fortress (with stamps of II Augusta and VI Victrix) argues for occupation.

events.title: Death of Septimius Severus at Eboracum
events.summary: Severus died of illness, probably gout-related, at York aged 65, leaving his sons as joint emperors with the advice, per Dio, to 'agree with each other, enrich the soldiers and scorn all others'.
events.detail: His ashes were carried in a porphyry urn to the Mausoleum of Hadrian. Severus' reign, dominated by the army, the jurists and the Syrian-African court, is often taken as the hinge between the Principate and the third-century military monarchy, though Millar and others emphasise continuity in the civil administration.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.title: Caracalla murders Geta
events.summary: After ten months of joint rule, during which the brothers divided the palace and reportedly considered splitting the empire, Caracalla had centurions kill Geta in the arms of their mother Julia Domna.
events.detail: Caracalla claimed to have foiled a plot and rushed to the Praetorian camp with a large donative. Dio says 20,000 of Geta's household and partisans were killed; Geta suffered a thorough damnatio memoriae, his face scraped from the Severan Tondo and his name chiselled from inscriptions across the empire. The jurist Papinian was executed in 212, reportedly for refusing to compose a justification of the murder.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.debate: Date sometimes given as 19 December or February 212; 26 December 211 is the most common reconstruction from the Chronograph of 354.

events.title: Constitutio Antoniniana: citizenship for all free inhabitants
events.summary: Caracalla granted Roman citizenship to virtually all free inhabitants of the empire, excepting only the dediticii; Dio says the real motive was to extend the 5% inheritance tax (raised to 10%) and the manumission tax.
events.detail: The edict survives in a damaged Greek copy on P.Giss. 40, in which Caracalla thanks the gods for his preservation (probably from Geta's 'plot') and offers citizenship to the inhabitants of the oikoumene. Hundreds of thousands of new citizens took the nomen Aurelius, which makes third-century prosopography a sea of Aurelii. Long-term consequences included the gradual displacement of local legal systems by Roman law (though local practice persisted, as Egyptian papyri show), the collapse of the citizen/peregrine distinction in the army and the hardening of the honestiores/humiliores divide as the main legal status line. The exact scope of the dediticii exclusion is one of the most debated cruxes in Roman legal history.
events.debate: Date (212 or 213), identity of the dediticii, whether P.Giss. 40 is the edict itself, and motive (fiscal, religious thanksgiving, ideological unification) are all disputed.

events.title: Caracalla's campaign against the Alamanni
events.summary: Caracalla crossed the Raetian limes in August 213 and defeated a Germanic coalition near the Main, taking the title Germanicus Maximus; Dio's account contains the first apparent mention of the Alamanni.
events.detail: The Acta of the Arval Brethren record sacrifices on 11 August 213 for Caracalla's entry into barbarian territory through Raetia. The victory was followed by payments to tribes, which Dio criticises. Whether the name Alamanni in Dio's text is original or inserted by the Byzantine excerptor Xiphilinus is a well-known controversy; Drinkwater argues the Alamanni as a people coalesced only in the later third century.
events.locName: Beyond the Raetian limes, Main region

events.title: Introduction of the antoninianus
events.summary: Caracalla introduced a new silver coin, the radiate 'antoninianus', apparently tariffed at two denarii but weighing only about 1.5 denarii, a concealed debasement to fund army pay.
events.detail: The denarius itself had already fallen to around 50% silver under Severus after his pay rise. The antoninianus (a modern name; its ancient name is uncertain, perhaps argenteus Antoninianus) was dropped under Severus Alexander and revived in 238, after which it drove out the denarius. Repeated debasement reduced it to under 5% silver by 268-270, the core of the third-century monetary collapse.
scholarship: Walker, The Metrology of the Roman Silver Coinage III (1978)
Estiot, in Metcalf (ed.), Oxford Handbook of Greek and Roman Coinage (2012)
events.debate: The face value of the antoninianus (two denarii is the usual but unproven assumption) is disputed.

events.title: Caracalla's massacre at Alexandria
events.summary: Offended by Alexandrian lampoons mocking him as a fratricide and his pretensions to be Alexander, Caracalla had the city's youths assembled for supposed recruitment into a phalanx and massacred, then expelled non-resident Egyptians.
events.detail: Dio and Herodian both describe thousands killed. A papyrus (P.Giss. 40 col. II) preserves Caracalla's order expelling Egyptian peasants from Alexandria, except those engaged in trade or worship, with the line that true Egyptians can be recognised by their speech and manners. The Museum's scholars lost their privileges.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.title: Baths of Caracalla dedicated
events.summary: The Thermae Antoninianae on the Via Appia, begun by Severus around 211, were dedicated in 216; the central block covered c. 2.5 hectares and could serve perhaps 1,600 bathers at once.
events.detail: The complex contained libraries, a natatio, and colossal sculptures such as the Farnese Bull and Farnese Hercules. Its frigidarium vaults and brick-faced concrete remained the model for later imperial baths, including those of Diocletian.

events.title: Caracalla's invasion of Parthia
events.summary: After Artabanus IV refused Caracalla's request to marry his daughter (a project to unite the two empires, according to Herodian), Caracalla invaded Media and Adiabene in 216, sacking towns and desecrating the royal tombs at Arbela.
events.detail: Herodian's tale of Caracalla massacring Parthian wedding guests is probably invented; Dio's version has Artabanus refusing outright. Caracalla advanced from Edessa, where he wintered, and planned a new campaign for 217 when he was murdered.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.title: Assassination of Caracalla near Carrhae
events.summary: Travelling from Edessa to the temple of the Moon god at Carrhae, Caracalla dismounted to relieve himself and was stabbed by the guardsman Julius Martialis, acting for the praetorian prefect Macrinus, who feared exposure by an astrologer's prophecy.
events.detail: Martialis was killed by Scythian bodyguards. After three days of uncertainty the army acclaimed Macrinus on 11 April, the first equestrian emperor, who had never sat in the Senate. Julia Domna, at Antioch, starved herself to death.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.title: Battle of Nisibis
events.summary: Artabanus IV invaded Mesopotamia to avenge Caracalla's attacks and fought Macrinus near Nisibis for three days; the outcome was bloody and inconclusive, and Macrinus bought peace with 200 million sesterces.
events.detail: Herodian says the Parthian cataphracts and camel-riders were hampered by caltrops strewn by the Romans, and that the field was so heaped with bodies the armies could not see each other. The payment, presented as gifts, was the last major Roman-Arsacid settlement: within seven years Artabanus was dead and the Sasanians ruled Iran.

battle.significance: Last great Roman-Arsacid battle; Macrinus' payment damaged his standing with the troops.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.debate: Some (on Herodian's account) count it a Parthian victory.

events.title: Revolt of Elagabalus at Raphanea
events.summary: Julia Maesa, sister of Julia Domna, had her fourteen-year-old grandson Varius Avitus Bassianus, priest of the sun god Elagabal at Emesa, presented to Legio III Gallica at Raphanea as Caracalla's bastard son; the troops proclaimed him emperor as 'Marcus Aurelius Antoninus'.
events.detail: Maesa's wealth (distributed freely), the boy's resemblance to Caracalla and dissatisfaction with Macrinus' pay cuts for new recruits all played a part. The eunuch Gannys organised the coup.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.title: Battle of Antioch (Immae)
events.summary: Macrinus' Praetorians were winning against the army of Elagabalus at a village about 180 stades from Antioch when Macrinus fled the field; his son Diadumenianus was caught and killed and Macrinus himself was captured in Cappadocia and executed.
events.detail: Dio describes Julia Maesa and Julia Soaemias leaping from their chariots to rally the wavering Elagabalan troops and the boy emperor charging with drawn sword. Macrinus fled disguised, shaved his head and beard, and got as far as Chalcedon.

battle.significance: Restored the Severan house through its Syrian female line.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus
